Pune, keeps meticulous weekly production records to monitor its output efficiency. The factory
operates under an internal benchmark of 1,200 cycles per week, which was set by the
management as the minimum threshold for profitable operation. Each cycle manufactured at
the unit is priced at 71,500 at the factory gate.
According to the production log maintained over five consecutive weeks, the factory produced
700 cycles in the 1st week, a figure that fell significantly below the internal benchmark.
Performance improved sharply in the 2nd week, with output rising to 1,400 cycles, more than
doubling the previous week's production. However, the 3rd week witnessed a dip, with only
1,000 cycles produced, followed by a further decline to 900 cycles in the 4th week. The factory

cycles — the highest weekly output and the only week to exceed the y-axis maximum of 1,600
on the production chart.
The management observed that production remained inconsistent across the period, with the
first and fourth weeks falling considerably below the benchmark while only the second and
fifth weeks managed to surpass it. The finance team was tasked with preparing a revenue
analysis based on these five weeks of production data to present before the board at the next
quarterly review.

importance of addressing such issues, the Court questioned whether the regulations might
unintentionally create further divisions.

framework to continue until further review.

Why am I in this car?
I'll sit still. Sometimes, if you don't move, your memory comes back.
But it's not working. One thing is certain, the driver is smoking. The vehicle is filled with

shoulders. On the rearview mirror a small cross is swinging on a string of pearls.

and then you lie awake and have to go to the bathroom every half an hour. Sometimes there
are visitors, but never for me. Sometimes someone dies and is taken away. But those who are
still alive are not usually picked up by a black car with a chauffeur.

slowly. The driver rolls down the window and yells that another war would do young punks

ranting.

questions.stimulus:
XI.	I speak to maps. And sometimes they say something back to me. This is not as strange as it
sounds, nor is it an unheard of thing. Before maps the world was limitless. It was maps that
gave it shape and made it seem like territory, like something that could be possessed, not just
laid to waste and plundered. Maps made places on the edges of the imagination seem
graspable and placeable. And later when it became necessary, geography became biology in
order to construct a hierarchy in which to place the people who lived in their inaccessibility
and primitiveness in other places on the map.
The first map I saw, though I must have seen others in innocence before that, was one a
teacher showed us when we were seven years old. I was seven anyway, even if I can't say for

certain about the ages of the multitude which shared this experience with me. There or
thereabouts, anyway. For some reason, you had to be below a certain age before you could
begin school. I have never properly considered the oddness of this before and it is only now as I
think it that I realise its strangeness. If you were over a certain age, it was as if you had gone
over the point beyond which you could be instructed, like a coconut that had overripened and
become undrinkable, or cloves that had been left too long on the tree and had swollen into
seeds. And even now as I think of it I can't come up with an explanation for this stern
exclusion. The British brought us school, and brought the rules to make school work. If the
rules said you had to be six and no older than six to be allowed to start school, that was how it
would be. Not that the schools had things their own way, because parents shaved off however
many years it was necessary to have their children allowed in. Birth certificate? They were
poor, ignorant people and never bothered to obtain one. Which was why they wanted their son
to go to school, so he wouldn't end up a beast like them.
Source: Excerpts from By the Sea and The Last Gift by Abdulrazak Gurnah

questions.stimulus:
XII. _—_ Erika doesn't want a silence to develop, so she utters a platitude. Art is platitudinous for Erika
because she lives off art. How much easier it is for the artist, says the woman, to hurl feelings
or passions out of himself. When an artist resorts to dramatic devices, which you so greatly
esteem, Klemmer, he is simply utilizing bogus methods while neglecting authentic ones. She
talks to prevent the eruption of silence. I, as a teacher, favor undramatic art -- Schumann, for
instance. Drama is always easier! Feelings and passions are always merely a substitute, a
surrogate for spirituality. The teacher yearns for an earthquake, for a roaring, raging tempest
to pounce upon her. That wild Klemmer is so angry that he almost drills his head into the
wall. The clarinet class next door, which he, the owner of a second instrument, has been
frequenting twice a week, would certainly be astonished if Klemmer's angry head suddenly
emerged from the wall, next to Beethoven's death mask. Oh, that Erika, that Erika. She
doesn't sense that he is actually talking about her, and naturally about himself as well! He is
connecting Erika and himself in a sensual context, ejecting the spirit, that enemy of the
senses, that primal foe of the flesh. She thinks he is referring to Schubert, but he really means
himself, just as he always means himself whenever he speaks. www.lawpreptutorial.com
He suddenly ventures to adopt a familiar tone with Erika; using a formal tone, she advises
him to remain objective! Her mouth puckers, willy-nilly, into a wrinkly rosette; she cannot
control it. She controls what the mouth says, but she cannot control the way it presents itself
to the outside world. She gets goosebumps all over.

XIV. There's a trill of heightened pleasure when you return to a film you had seen and enjoyed years
ago, a pleasure that lies somewhere between memory and discovery. The first viewing is an
initiation - plot twists, characters and images strike with the force of novelty. But the second time,
the film becomes a familiar room you re-enter, where every corner holds echoes of your past self.
Rewatching something you enjoyed is not repetition; it's extraction and enrichment. You savour the
anticipation of scenes you know are coming - the witty line, the sudden silence, swell of music. And,
yet, they arrive with fresh resonance. Memory and present experience overlap, creating a double
exposure of delight.
You recall where you were when you first saw it, who you were, even what you felt. And then you
feel it again, layered with the wisdom of time.
There is also the luxury of noticing what was missed: the flicker of an expression, a background
detail, the rhythm of editing. The film, once consumed in haste, now unfolds like a slow meal. To
rewatch is to both indulge in nostalgia and uncover new pleasures. It is bliss precisely because you
reckon this is what being inexhaustible is like.

XV.	The Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, popularly known as the Anti-Defection Law, was
introduced to combat the evil of political defections motivated by the lure of office or material
advantage. However, recent political crises across various states have exposed glaring loopholes in
its architecture. The law designates the Speaker of the legislative assembly as the sole adjudicator
of defection petitions. This creates an inherent conflict of interest, as the Speaker is almost always
a member of the ruling party and depends on their goodwill for continuance in office. Consequently,
adjudication is often marred by partisan bias. Petitions against opposition members are decided
with remarkable haste, whereas those against ruling party legislators are kept pending
indefinitely, effectively defeating the law's purpose.
Furthermore, the 'merger' exception under paragraph 4 of the Schedule allows a two-thirds
majority of a legislature party to merge with another party without facing disqualification.
Originally intended to protect genuine ideological realignments, this provision is now frequently
weaponized to engineer wholesale defections. Critics argue that this legitimizes retail defection
while merely raising the threshold to wholesale defection. To restore constitutional morality, legal
experts advocate stripping the Speaker of this adjudicatory power. Instead, an independent
tribunal headed by retired judges or the Election Commission should decide disqualification
matters. While the Supreme Court has repeatedly urged Parliament to amend the Constitution to
effect this change, legislative inertia persists. Until the institutional mechanism is overhauled, the
Tenth Schedule will remain a tool for political maneuvering rather than a shield against it.
Source: Edited and Excerpted from:
https://prsindia.org/files/parliament/discussion_papers/The_Anti-Defection_Law.pdf

XVI. Assam and Puducherry recorded historically the highest, and Kerala close to the highest, turnout
in Assembly elections held on April 9. In Assam, 85.91% of the electorate turned up to vote, while
in Puducherry it was over 91.23% and in Kerala, 78.27%. It is hazardous to pinpoint the reasons for
high turnouts and treacherous to read meanings into them. However, some reasons are objectively
identifiable and some meaningful conjectures can be made. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of
the electoral rolls in Puducherry and Kerala culled considerable numbers of names - 7.5% and
3.2%, respectively. In Assam, given that a process for the creation of a National Register of Citizens
for the State is under way, it was a Special Revision which is a less rigorous updating of the rolls
that led to its shrinking by less than 1%. The smaller size of the denominator - the size of the
electorate - is one reason why the turnout percentages are high. Ghost voters and duplicate entries
may have been eliminated in the process. Another reason for the higher turnout is that due to
intense concerns regarding potential disenfranchisement around the SIR/SR, voters may have
taken a keener interest in turning up at the booth. In Assam, for instance, large numbers of
migrant voters travelled home to vote. In Kerala, anecdotal reporting suggests that its migrant
voters from West Asia who travel during polling season could not do so this time due to the ongoing
war.

questions.stimulus:
SECTION V
XVII. In criminal law, the distinction between intention, knowledge, and negligence determines not
only the quantum of punishment but the very character of the offense. Intention involves a
conscious, deliberate objective to bring about a specific consequence. Knowledge exists when
an individual is practically certain that a consequence will result from their actions, even if
that result is not their primary aim. Negligence, however, rests on the breach of a duty to take
reasonable care; harmful consequences arise because the actor failed to exercise the caution
legally expected of them in those circumstances.
The law differentiates these mental states because the moral blameworthiness is distinct. A
person who deliberately inflicts injury cannot be equated with one who inadvertently creates
risk. However, criminal negligence requires a significantly higher threshold than civil
negligence. For an act to constitute criminal negligence-such as under Section 106 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (formerly Section 304A IPC)-there must be a high degree of
disregard for human life and safety. The conduct must exhibit gross neglect or rashness, going
far beyond a mere error of judgment or ordinary carelessness.
Context is heavily determinative. Undertaking inherently dangerous activities-such as
performing complex surgery, handling hazardous substances, or operating heavy machinery-
imposes a higher standard of care because the foreseeable risks are severe. Yet, a tragic
outcome res ipsa loquitur (the thing speaks for itself) does not automatically establish criminal
liability. Courts must meticulously examine what the accused knew, what precautions were
reasonably feasible, and whether the lapse in judgment crossed the stringent threshold into
criminal culpability. www.lawpreptutorial.com

including Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and principles governing Sections 299, 300, and

questions.stimulus:
XVIII. In contract law, not every statement made during negotiations becomes a binding term of the
contract. A statement may be a mere representation, intended to induce the other party into
entering the agreement, or it may be a contractual promise, breach of which gives rise to
liability irrespective of fraud. The distinction depends on several factors: the importance
attached to the statement, the relative knowledge of the parties, the timing between the
statement and the contract, and whether the statement was reduced into writing. Where one
party possesses special knowledge and the other relies substantially on that assertion, the law
is more inclined to treat the statement as a term rather than casual sales talk.
This distinction has important consequences. If the statement forms part of the contract, its
falsity may amount to breach even where the maker honestly believed it to be true. If it is
merely a representation, the remedy may depend on whether the misstatement was
fraudulent, negligent, or innocent. However, the law also recognizes that exaggerated
commendation, obvious opinion, or statements not intended to be taken literally do not
ordinarily create contractual obligations. Similarly, where the representee independently
verifies the facts or expressly agrees not to rely solely on pre-contractual assertions, the legal
effect of the statement may weaken.
Courts therefore examine not merely what was said, but the commercial setting in which it
was said. The law seeks to protect genuine reliance, but it does not convert every failed
expectation into breach of contract. Much turns on whether the statement was meant to
allocate risk, and whether a reasonable person in that situation would have understood it as
contractually binding.
Source: Inspired by classic common law principles reflected in Oscar Chess Ltd v Williams,
Dick Bentley Productions Ltd v Harold Smith (Motors) Lid, and Indian Contract Act doctrines
on consent, misrepresentation, and contractual terms.

contract. A statement may be a mere representation, intended to induce the other party into
entering the agreement, or it may be a contractual promise, breach of which gives rise to

statement and the contract, and whether the statement was reduced into writing. Where one

questions.stimulus:
XX. International criminal law differentiates atrocities not merely by the scale of the violence, but
by the specific intent and context of the acts. Under the Rome Statute of the International
Criminal Court (ICC), the three primary core crimes are Genocide, Crimes Against Humanity,
and War Crimes. While these categories often overlap in armed conflicts, their legal thresholds
remain distinct. The crime of genocide, originally codified in the 1948 Genocide Convention
and mirrored in Article 6 of the Rome Statute, is uniquely defined by dolus specialis-a specific
intent. To constitute genocide, acts such as killing, causing serious bodily harm, or forcibly
transferring children must be committed with the explicit "Intent to destroy, in whole or in
part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such". The destruction of political or
cultural groups does not fall under this strict definition. Crucially, the prosecution must prove
that the victims were targeted primarily because of their membership in one of the four
protected groups, not merely as a byproduct of conflict. Conversely, Crimes Against Humanity
(Article 7 of the Rome Statute) do not require the specific intent to destroy a group. Instead,
acts like murder, torture, deportation, or apartheid must be committed as part of a
"widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population". Unlike war crimes,
crimes against humanity can be prosecuted even if they occur during peacetime or are
committed by a State against its own citizens. The requirement of a "widespread or
systematic" attack ensures that isolated or random acts of violence, however heinous, do not
trigger international jurisdiction. War Crimes (Article 8) are violations of international
humanitarian law, particularly the Geneva Conventions. They are strictly contextual,
meaning they can only occur within an armed conflict, whether international or non-
international. War crimes focus on the unlawful conduct of hostilities-such as intentionally
targeting civilians, attacking hospitals, or torturing prisoners of war-irrespective of whether
the violence aims to destroy a specific ethnic group or is part of a widespread attack.

questions.stimulus:
XXI. Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to equality, but it does not mandate
absolute, mathematical equality where everyone is treated identically in every single
situation. The law recognizes that society is diverse, and treating fundamentally unequal
people in the exact same way can actually result in injustice. Therefore, the State is permitted
to classify citizens into different categories and apply different rules to them, provided the
classification is legally "reasonable." www.lawpreptutorial.com
For a legal classification to be valid and constitutional, it must pass a strict two-step test.
First, it must be based on an "intelligible differentia." This means there must be a clear,
logical, and recognizable distinguishing factor that separates the people included in the group
from those left out. Second, there must be a "rational nexus." This requires that the
distinguishing factor must have a direct, logical connection to the specific objective the
government is trying to achieve through that law.

If a law fails either part of this test, it is termed "class legislation," which is unconstitutional.
For example, a law taxing businesses earning over 210 crore at a higher rate passes the test:
the income level is a clear difference (intelligible differentia), and it logically connects to the
goal of wealth redistribution (rational nexus). However, a law taxing businesses differently
based on the owner's hair color would fail; while hair color is a clear difference, it has
absolutely no logical connection to economic policy or tax collection.
Furthermore, courts have established that Article 14 also forbids "manifest arbitrariness."
Even if a law applies equally to everyone, if the rule itself is completely irrational, whimsical,
or lacks any guiding public principle, it violates the fundamental right to equality.
Source: Inspired by Article 14 of the Constitution of India and landmark Supreme Court
judgments defining the "Two-Test Rule" of reasonable classification (State of West Bengal v.
Anwar Ali Sarkar) and the doctrine of manifest arbitrariness (Shayara Bano v. Union of
India).
